sources.citation: Bradley, David. 1977. Phunoi or Côông. In D. Bradley (ed.), Papers in South-East Asian Linguistics No. 5 (Pacific Linguistics A-49), 67-98. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-A49.67. https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/handle/1885/254373
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Nothing: the phonetics/phonology section (pp. 69-72) gives 'Minor Syllables (schwa vowel, pitch same as following syllable..)' (p. 69) and '5. Tones.. High (level or slightly falling), low (level or slightly falling), mid (level), and rising, phonetically. The rising tone does not occur in the primary system.' (p. 70); the words stress/accent do not occur in the chapter (checked in the repository text layer and extracted text).

sources.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 1980. Le verbe en phounoy. Cahiers de Linguistique - Asie Orientale 8: 113-133. DOI 10.3406/clao.1980.1082. https://www.persee.fr/doc/clao_0153-3320_1980_num_8_1_1082
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. 'II. Phonologie sommaire' (pp. 114-116): three main tones (haut plain, moyen plain non marqué, bas descendant) plus marginal tones; p. 115: the word is minimally monosyllabic 'consonne initiale, une voyelle et un ton'; disyllabic words have a 'présyllabe' pronounced on a mid tone whose vowel 'n'a pas de timbre pertinent'; phrase-final demarcative glottalisation. No occurrence of 'accent'.

sources.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 2019. Lexique phounoy-français. Preprint, HAL halshs-02188910. https://shs.hal.science/halshs-02188910
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Introduction (unpaginated, PDF p. 4): consonant and vowel charts, 'Tons principaux a¹ a² a³ (finales sonores) / a¹ a³ (finales sourdes -p -t -ʔ)', 'Structure syllabique: En phounoy le mot est monosyllabique CV(C), ou semi-syllabique C.CV(C).' One entry note: 'le ton de la présyllabe est nettement haut'. No occurrence of 'accent'.

sources.citation: Edmondson, Jerold A. 2005 [2002]. The Central and Southern Loloish languages of Vietnam. Proceedings of BLS 28, Special Session on Tibeto-Burman and Southeast Asian Linguistics, 1-13. https://journals.linguisticsociety.org/proceedings/index.php/BLS/article/view/1042
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: First-hand on Côông of Vietnam (coon1239, a separate Glottolog language), second-hand on Phunoi from Bradley 1977/1979. Comparison table p. 3: Phunoi 'minor syllables take the tone of the main syllable but has no independent tone' vs Côông 'first syllable is often unstressed but has independent tone'; pp. 4-5: 'Phunoi minor syllables possess a limited inventory of initials, schwa vowels, and a tone the same as the following main syllable. Côông word structure has some features of a weak first syllable; it is, for example, iambic with a somewhat shortened first vowel for many words.' No stress…
